title: How Should a Pastor Manage His Calendar and Time?
subtitle: Why the calendar, and not the sermon, is the truest confession of what a pastor believes

sections.title: Your Calendar Is a Theology
sections.body:
Show me your week and I will tell you what you believe. Not what you preached on Sunday. What you believed on Tuesday at two in the afternoon, when the phone rang and the email arrived and the man at the door needed twenty minutes that became ninety.

We say the work of God is prayer and the Word. We say it from the pulpit. Then we spend the week on the parking lot dispute, the broken copier, the committee that cannot decide on a carpet color. The mouth confesses one thing. The calendar confesses another. And the calendar is not lying.

Charles Hummel named this in 1967, in a small booklet most pastors have never read. The tyranny of the urgent. The urgent is not the important. The urgent is merely loud. It stands at your door with its hand already raised, and the important sits quietly in the corner waiting for a meeting you will reschedule three times and finally cancel. I have canceled it. I am not writing to you from above this. I am writing to you from inside it.

sections.title: The Work Anyone Can Do
sections.body:
Here is the hard line to draw, and you must draw it with a pencil pressed down hard. There is work only you can do. And there is work anyone could do. The tragedy of most pastoral weeks is that the second devours the first and calls it ministry.

No one else can pray for your people the way the shepherd prays. No one else can sit with the dying woman and not look at his watch. No one else can wrestle the text until Thursday until it gives up its weight, so that Sunday is bread and not crumbs. That is the work only you can do.

Anybody can answer the email. Anybody can chase the contractor. Anybody can sit in the third meeting about the budget for the nursery paint. I am not saying those things do not matter. I am saying they do not require you, and every hour you give them is an hour stolen from the woman who is dying and the text that has not yet broken open. We tell ourselves we are being faithful. We are being busy. They are not the same. They have never been the same.

sections.title: Build the Wall Before the Flood
sections.body:
You cannot protect the morning by hoping for the morning. Hope is not a fence. You protect it by deciding, in advance, in writing, that from eight to noon the door is closed and the phone is dark and the sermon gets your first and best hours while you still have first and best hours to give.

I know a pastor who studied at nine at night for fifteen years because that was the only time left after the day had eaten him. He preached tired sermons to tired people and wondered why nothing moved. His problem was not his theology. His problem was his schedule. He gave God his exhaustion and the church his prime, and he had it exactly backward.

Protect the block, and the world will test it within the week. Someone will need you. Someone always needs you. And you will have to decide whether the urgent man at the door is a genuine emergency or simply a loud one, because most are loud and few are emergencies, and the discernment between those two is itself a pastoral skill you will spend your whole life learning. Guard the morning. Let the afternoon take the noise.

sections.title: Every Yes Is Married to a No
sections.body:
We preach a gospel of grace and then live a schedule of works. We say yes to everything because we cannot bear to be the one who let someone down, and so we let everyone down a little, slowly, for years.

Every yes you say is married to a no you did not notice. Yes to the fourth meeting is no to your son's game. Yes to the denominational committee three counties over is no to the new believer who needed an hour this week and will not ask twice. The no is invisible. That is why it is dangerous. You never see the thing you sacrificed, so you never count the cost, and the uncounted cost is the one that bankrupts you.

Eugene Peterson said the pastor who is always available is not available to anyone, because availability without boundaries is not love. It is the inability to disappoint, dressed up as devotion. I have worn that costume. It fit me well for years. It nearly cost me my family before I learned that a man who cannot say no does not actually have anything to give, only a long line of people he is failing in order of arrival.

sections.title: What You Will Answer For
sections.body:
You will not stand before God and give an account of your inbox. You will not be asked how quickly you returned calls. The metrics that ran your week will not appear on the scale that measures your life.

You will be asked whether you fed the sheep. Whether you knew them. Whether the man who was drowning got the shepherd or got the voicemail. Whether the Word you carried was alive in you or merely processed through you on the way to a deadline.

The calendar is the most honest document you own. More honest than your journal, because the journal records what you wished and the calendar records what you did. Open it. Read it as a confession. And then change it, not because productivity is holy, but because the people God gave you cannot be loved by a man whose hours are spent on everything except them.

The urgent will be at your door tomorrow. It is always at the door. The question is whether you will answer it before you have done the one thing it was sent to interrupt.
